# BGRA and DDS Compatibility Migration Workflow

This page preserves an old migration path, not an overview of the current image API. The reading entry point is still `UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleSprite.cs`. Early investigations started here because raw BGRA images, sprite objects, and DDS wrappers appeared in the same compatibility issue; it was later found that presenting them as a single straight line obscured two separate checks: object identity and blank pixels.

The diagram from the previous version can still be used to locate the points of disagreement at the time:

```text
Old assessment
Raw image → DDS wrapper → Can continue processing

Separate records after review
Raw image → DDS wrapper → First result
                         └→ Result of processing again, assessed separately
```

“Can continue processing” in the diagram was once treated as a signal that migration was complete. That interpretation is now useful only for explaining why wrapper round-tripping was listed as a risk at the time. It did not establish whether the raw image already had usable pixel content when it was created, or whether the conversion operation created a new object. The old procedure is therefore retained, but it cannot be used as a reason to skip checking the original object.

When handling this old path, first split the issue into two records. One covers the raw image's creation, blank pixels, and conversion; the other covers whether processing can be started again after the DDS wrapper is generated. Even when the first result is normal, the outcome for the second record should still be recorded. If the second processing attempt does not succeed, the fallback is to stop using that result as a basis for approval and return to the image object before wrapping to continue investigating; do not modify the original object to make the wrapper look acceptable.

There is an easily overlooked point in the original migration sequence: retaining the raw image is not just for comparing the displayed output afterward. The object before wrapping is the only place to determine whether creation and conversion changed the image's identity. Once the object has been passed to the DDS wrapper, inferring this stage from the wrapped result conflates pixel state, object identity, and the wrapper's own result into a single conclusion. The record should therefore describe what happened to the original object first, and only then what happened to the wrapper output.

This review adds the previously missing creation boundary. A newly allocated GMImage(3, 2) is RawBgra, writes 24 zero bytes for blank pixels, and ConvertToRawBgra returns the same object when it is already raw BGRA.

This fact changes the original order of checks. A blank image does not acquire its pixel state only after DDS wrapping; it should be treated as raw BGRA from creation. A blank object with dimensions 3×2 has explicitly defined zero-byte pixel content and cannot be treated merely as an unfilled placeholder object. For an object that is already raw BGRA, conversion is not an opportunity to replace the object either. Therefore, when recording a round trip, retain the observation of whether the same object continues to be used, rather than simply writing “conversion succeeded”.

The old migration instructions recommended generating the wrapper first, then deciding whether to retain the original object. That recommendation no longer applies: it can easily allow the wrapper result to obscure blank pixels and object identity. Now, first confirm the raw image state, then generate the DDS wrapper; after wrapping is complete, test separately whether that result can be processed again. The two observations address different questions and cannot cancel each other out.

This does not make the DDS wrapper an irrelevant step. For the old path, it remains an intermediate object whose result must be recorded. The first result after wrapping can show that this step was completed, but it does not automatically show that its output can serve as input for the next processing attempt. Only by restarting processing from that output can a record be obtained for the “wrapper round trip” side. If the second processing attempt does not succeed, keep the failure localized to the stage after the wrapper result, rather than going back and modifying the already verified raw BGRA object.

The retained fallback paths are as follows:

- When the raw image state does not match expectations, stop at creation and conversion, and do not proceed to assess the wrapper round trip. In this case, the first result from DDS should not be used in place of a record of blank pixels or object identity.
- When the raw state matches expectations but the DDS result cannot be processed again, retain the original object and the first result, and withdraw the old assumption that “the wrapper can continue processing”. Continue investigating the wrapped object; do not attribute the issue to a failure to create the raw image successfully.
- If the first wrapped result was not retained, even reproducing the displayed output later does not allow the original round trip to be retroactively recorded as passed. A new round of separate records can be made, but objects from the new round should not be mixed into the old migration results.
- Use the example as a reference for this old migration path only when results have been recorded on both sides; it still does not represent other dimensions or other DDS variants.

“Different dimensions” remains an open question here because the current creation boundary covers only a blank image of 3×2. This is enough to correct the old claim that blank pixels are left entirely to the wrapper to handle, but it cannot provide the same record for other dimensions. DDS variants remain unresolved at the same point: this page has no material that would justify generalizing the result of a particular wrapper round trip to all variants.

One related issue has not yet been moved off this page: the shortest real example of a DDS wrapper round trip should be selected from existing regression cases, and it should be verified whether the first result can still be processed again. No sample is fabricated here, and normal display is not treated as a substitute result. The selected example should allow the original object before wrapping, the first wrapped result, and the result of the second processing attempt all to be retained; otherwise, it can establish only one segment and cannot support a judgment about the entire migration path.

This record therefore remains useful for explaining why the old path is split into two segments and which segment to fall back to when something goes wrong. It is no longer suitable for supporting the judgment that “successful wrapping means migration is complete”. The old diagram and wording are retained so that readers arriving from the old investigation entry point can see that the creation boundary was what had been missed, rather than mistakenly assuming that the DDS wrapper itself had already been proven problem-free.

# Decision on Boolean Checks and LTS Requirements

In the 2024.6 compatibility train, Boolean equivalence checks and LTS branch version status were grouped into the same batch of compatibility issues, but they should not be recorded as a single check result. The former needs to be traced back to call sites that still use the check; the latter needs specific branch and version examples.

Three approaches were compared at the time: fold LTS status into Boolean check regression coverage; keep two check tracks and list them side by side when organizing regression coverage; leave them together until a new failing sample appears. The second approach was chosen.

Combining them would mistake version status for a side effect of expression behavior. Leaving them together would keep subsequent investigations starting from the issue name, with no way to tell whether to find the caller first or add version tests first. Both tracks can appear in the same compatibility review, but one sample cannot establish a conclusion for the other.

For Boolean equivalence checks, retain the caller, the version it was running on, the entry point into the check, and the result at the time. For LTS branch version status, add repository tests based on user-reported examples; if there is a failure, retain the failure text or output bytes.

The old investigation notes point to UndertaleModLib/Compiler/Parser.cs as a starting point for reading. Use that file first to review related references and historical behavior; do not treat the path itself as a shared implementation point for the two requirements.

versions.body:
# Decision on Boolean Checks and LTS Requirements

This record began with a classification dispute in the 2024.6 compatibility train. Boolean equivalence checks and the version status of the LTS branch appeared in the same batch of regression questions, and the old records directed readers toward the compiler in both cases, making it easy to treat them as a single compatibility conclusion awaiting confirmation. The initial draft's decision was not to label a particular version, but to first separate what each question addressed.

This addendum retains the choices made in the initial draft and adds the entry points that each track later acquired during actual verification. Both matters can still emerge from the same round of regression review, but the record must make the distinction clear to future readers: caller verification answers what result a check produced at a particular entry point and version; version example testing answers whether the user-reported LTS branch status has been captured in inspectable material in the repository.

## Choices Retained from the Initial Draft

Three options were initially proposed.

The first was to treat the version status of the LTS branch as one result of the boolean equivalence check. Its apparent advantage was that only one regression item needed to be maintained: find where the check is used, then record the observed behavior on the same line. That was also the problem. A call site can establish the version, entry point, and current result at that location, but cannot establish a conclusion about the branch status in the user report. If the version example later needs a separate test, the merged entry cannot explain what needs to be added.

The second was to retain two inspection targets, listed side by side in the compatibility train's regression review. Evidence for boolean equivalence checks would be recorded by caller; evidence for the version status of the LTS branch would be recorded by version example. They could be verified at the same time and appear in the same release materials, but neither side's results could be inferred from the other's.

The third was to leave them together for now and wait for a new failure sample before deciding. This approach avoided making overly broad statements when evidence was sparse, but did not provide a stable verification direction for the compatibility questions already raised. The next time someone saw only “boolean” or “LTS”, they would still have to work backward from the old issue name to guess which route to follow.

The second option was chosen. This decision addresses only the boundaries of recording and verification; it does not declare in advance that a particular caller, a particular LTS branch, or the entire train is already compatible. At the time, the initial draft had not retained enough call results, nor had it retained a version failure sample that could be reproduced here, so it did not present evidence still to be added as a conclusion.

## What Each Type of Evidence Answers

Evidence for boolean equivalence checks starts with the caller. A verification should at least identify which call site still uses the check, its actual version, where the inspection starts, and the result obtained at the time. Simply writing “a boolean equivalence check is used here” is not enough for later comparison: the same name may appear at different entry points, and retaining only the name loses the version and context.

Evidence for the version status of the LTS branch starts with the version example referenced in the user report. The example should be added as a repository test; if it still fails, retain the failure text or output bytes alongside the test materials. The concern here is the example's status once it has been added to the tests, not covering all versions with a blanket statement that “LTS works normally”. The report itself provides a starting point for investigation; the test gives subsequent verification something to continue examining.

The minimum record structure differs between the two sides. The caller side centers on entry points and results, while the version example side centers on branch status and test materials. Labeling both as “covered” would lose this distinction; treating a sample from either side as proof for the other would also make failures impossible to classify.

The initial draft once used a broader working statement: finding just one caller that still uses the boolean equivalence check would establish the shape of this regression item. That statement was suitable only as a starting point for finding samples, and was not retained as a sufficient basis for judgment. One caller can provide useful actual results, but those results still describe only its own location, version, and entry point.

Likewise, LTS status cannot be treated as a release marker following a boolean check. Branch version status needs to enter testing along with the version example; it is not an incidental conclusion drawn from the result of a particular expression check. The initial draft contained no evidence supporting that inference, so this broad statement was not extended further.

## Where to Start Reading Parser.cs

UndertaleModLib/Compiler/Parser.cs remains in this record because the old investigation directed readers here based on issue names and call names. It is suitable as a local starting point for reviewing historical behavior: first continue reading from references related to that file, then record the findings under the specific call sample.

This location does not serve as the test checklist for the version status of the LTS branch, nor does it automatically become the implementation location for both requirements. The old investigation provided a file from which to begin reading; the current verification must put the findings back under the correct record target. For boolean equivalence checks, results should go back to the caller entry; for LTS examples, results should go back to the corresponding test materials.

The repository index lists this path as an existing C# module for code reading and historical behavior checks. When revisiting old references, use v_prev of internal/undertale-core as the corresponding version entry point. Retaining the path this way preserves the starting point of the old investigation; it does not turn the filename into a substitute for a compatibility assessment.

## Two Later Verification Entry Points

UMT-207 recorded a caller_walkthrough. It brought “boolean equivalence check” back from a generic issue name to caller inspection: find call sites still using the check, then verify their actual version, entry point, and current result. This is consistent with the initial draft's decision to separate the tracks, and also shows why adding samples later should not mean merely adding the name of a check.

The local description of UMT-218 retained another work track: add repository tests from user-reported examples of the LTS branch's version status, and retain the current failure text or output bytes. The card subsequently underwent security_triaged, and was then recorded as work_started（To Do → In Progress）. These actions show that work on the relevant materials has begun, not that the tests have passed or that a final conclusion has been reached on branch status.

The two cards serve different purposes on this page. UMT-207 directs readers back to the callers awaiting verification; UMT-218 directs readers back to the version example tests that still need to be added. Both belong to this batch of compatibility work, but the actions recorded on the cards are not recast as technical conclusions here.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Registered Side by Side" as Registered
    state "Caller Verification" as Caller
    state "Version Examples Added to Tests" as LtsCase
    state "Regression Review" as Review

    [*] --> Registered
    Registered --> Caller: Boolean equivalence check
    Registered --> LtsCase: LTS branch version status
    Caller --> Review
    LtsCase --> Review
    Review --> [*]
```

The convergence point in the diagram means only that evidence from both tracks can enter regression review together, not that they have already reached the same conclusion before converging. Caller results still belong in caller records, and version example results still belong in test records. With this arrangement, readers entering through a regression item can find two distinct directions for follow-up questions, rather than seeing only one ambiguous compatibility status.

## Consolidation Approaches Not Adopted

Parser.cs was not designated as the sole checkpoint under a unified entry point. Doing so would make it appear that caller verification could begin only from one file, and would also misplace LTS test materials in the compilation-path narrative. The fact that the old investigation pointed to this file is worth retaining, but it answers only where to begin reading, not where each piece of evidence belongs.

Nor were the two tracks brought together under a shared pass/fail conclusion. The current result of a boolean equivalence check may come from a particular call site; the status of a LTS example may come from a repository test. They observe different targets, so even if neither shows anomalies in a particular review, their results can only be recorded separately.

The option of postponing the split was not reinstated either. There is now an entry point for caller verification and a clear direction for turning LTS examples into tests. Keeping them in a single, undivided item awaiting investigation would only leave new evidence without a fixed place.

This decision also does not cover decompiler compatibility or local declaration rendering status. That set of interface review materials is maintained in DOC-16; this page retains only the history of boolean equivalence checks and the version status of the LTS branch, to avoid turning the same batch of work into one unbounded topic.

## Current Recording Practice

1. When adding a boolean equivalence check sample, first specify the caller, actual version, entry point, and current result. If only a name or issue name has been found, retain it as a reading lead for now, rather than listing it as a regression result.

2. When adding evidence for the version status of the LTS branch, first confirm which user-reported version example it corresponds to, then add it to the repository tests. The failure text or output bytes should be saved with that example, rather than leaving only a “failed” summary in the rollup.

3. During regression review, the two tracks appear side by side. The summary may state which materials were examined in this round, but must not use one call sample to conclude version status, nor use one version test to draw conclusions about all call sites.

4. When revisiting the old reading path, continue searching from the relevant references to UndertaleModLib/Compiler/Parser.cs and v_prev. File the findings separately by caller or version test, rather than creating a third, mixed entry that duplicates them.

5. Cards serve only as navigation to the materials. UMT-207 corresponds to caller verification, and UMT-218 corresponds to LTS example testing; when more processing records are later added to a card, whether this decision needs to change depends on whether they change the recording boundaries between the two tracks, not on the card's status itself.

What is still missing is not a more complete overview, but concrete samples. The caller side has not yet retained actual results on this page; the LTS side has not retained complete failure text or output bytes here either. If a phenomenon later arises that involves both a call entry point and version status, retain a call sample and a version test separately, then determine whether the two sets of evidence point to the same actual relationship.

For now, no third “boolean and LTS combined” category will be added. Only when both the caller records and the version example tests clearly point to the same actual relationship is there reason to record them as sharing a common cause; until then, keeping them side by side is more faithful to the available evidence than merging them.

# Decompiler Compatibility Adjustment Proposal

This page was still used later to cross-check compatibility issues with 2024.6, but it records an interface trial, not a finalized decompiler specification. The review entry point remains `UndertaleModLib/Decompiler/Decompiler.cs`. Local declarations and their neighboring objects are visible here first; the early discussion placed both issues in this area, saving an initial search but also making the “shared state” assessment below sound more certain than it actually was.

> The approach in the initial draft: split-decompiler compatibility and local declaration rendering state share one context entry point. Processing after the split is determined by that same context; local declarations also obtain their rendering state from there. This keeps the change surface small and requires only one output comparison during investigation.
>
> The initial draft retained a rollback condition: if repeated processing and local declaration rendering produce results pointing in different directions, stop treating them as the same state issue.

The paragraphs above have not been removed. They explain why we leaned toward combining the two at the time: both issues appeared in the compatibility train, and both names referred to decompiler output. They did not become an interface conclusion. The later review found no basis for going directly from “nearby in the same file” to “the same rendering state,” so this round separates the trials rather than adding a larger shared switch.

First, distinguish the two observation points:

- **Split-decompiler compatibility** concerns whether the content or diagnostics for the same object remain stable after the first and subsequent processing passes. What we need to retain here is the difference between the two passes, not a predetermined requirement for what a particular text output must look like.
- **Local declaration rendering state** concerns the output the tool actually produces when source code that directly triggers local declaration rendering state goes through the existing entry point. This observation can be made in the same review round as the first, but its input, output, and assessment are saved independently.

This distinction also explains why “local declarations” are not treated as a sub-assertion of split compatibility. The former may manifest as source rendering; the latter may manifest as changes in content or diagnostics before and after processing. Even if both ultimately need to touch `Decompiler.cs`, one observation cannot be used to substantiate the other during the trial.

## The Two Remaining Candidates

**Candidate A: continue sharing the context entry point.**

The advantage is a concentrated set of changes. If all relevant calls already depend on the same context, local declaration state and the compatibility branch for split processing can be adjusted together. This was the direction taken in the initial draft.

The cost is that, when something fails, it is hard to tell where the change came from. A change in local declaration output might be incorrectly recorded as a side effect of split compatibility; unstable diagnostics from repeated processing might also be wrongly attributed to rendering state. This direction is worth pursuing only if two independent sets of samples actually show the same state boundary.

**Candidate B: retain the existing entry point and add observations and minimal adjustments independently.**

This approach does not assume that the two sides share fields, nor does it put compatibility checks into the declaration rendering path. Split processing compares only the first and subsequent passes; local declarations retain only the direct input and actual output. When changes are needed, try them within their respective local boundaries first, without expanding the changes for the sake of “interface unification.”

This round adopts B as the trial sequence. It does not claim that there will ultimately be two long-term interfaces; it simply gives the two failure modes their own samples first. Once the samples show a common state source, we can discuss whether to combine them. This decision is more conservative than the initial draft and also means we will not get a neat, unified entry point in the short term.

## Materials to Retain

The investigation items in UMT-208 require running the first and subsequent processing passes separately and recording whether the content or diagnostics remain stable. During review, retain the two results side by side; if a difference appears only on the second pass, label it as a repeated-processing boundary first, rather than immediately adding local declarations to the reproduction conditions.

UMT-211 require source code that directly triggers local declaration rendering state, along with the actual output produced when that input goes through the existing entry point. “Directly” matters here: the sample should not depend on an intermediate result already changed by split processing. If the behavior is visible only in a mixed path, record that mixed path; do not present it as an isolated reproduction for local declarations.

The caller's insertion of StringBuilder is still a separate boundary, handled under DOC-17. It may affect the final concatenated text, but it should not be used to establish where state belongs inside `Decompiler.cs`. Conversely, if a local declaration sample looks abnormal only after the caller's insertion, add that condition back to the sample first rather than forcing the issue into this proposal.

## Signals to Stop

If any of the following occurs, candidate B should not be presented as a completed design either:

- The difference between the first and subsequent processing passes cannot be reproduced consistently, or only diagnostic text remains, with no comparable content;
- The local declaration input cannot be saved independently of the mixed path, making it impossible to determine whether it really represents independent rendering state;
- Both sets of samples point to the caller's insertion of StringBuilder, with `Decompiler.cs` merely being passed through in the output chain;
- Making the samples pass requires first assuming an unconfirmed shared context.

The first three cases should stop at recording the findings, without adding an interface. The fourth directly withdraws the old “combine first, validate later” approach. Withdrawal only restores the separation of the issues; it does not require deleting the old paragraphs, which still explain why this page originally put the two names together.

Scope confirmation for UMT-208 was completed later, but that did not replace the samples. What is still missing is exactly which content repeated processing compares, what output the local declaration sample actually leaves under the existing entry point, and whether the two sides converge on the same local state. Only once these materials are complete will it be worth reopening this page's shared-entry-point draft.

# Buffer release Boundary Decision Record

This record was initially treated as a narrowly scoped window-side compatibility item: the earlier investigation left behind the issue name “buffer release boundary” and set `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` as the location to revisit. That link continued to be used later, so it was not deleted. It could take people to the file examined at the time, but it did not preserve the release call chain, object ownership, or reproduction conditions.

The initial draft favored the wording “window-side.” That was a trade-off made at the time to preserve the investigation entry point, not confirmation of the implementation location. Looking back now, the useful part of the old wording is that the filename and issue name still match up; the inaccurate part is that it can lead people to think the window file already explains when the buffer is released, who holds the read position, and where the exception is returned from. Those details were not recorded at the time.

## The Earlier Decision Retained

The initial draft effectively chose between two options.

- Delete this record outright and register it again once a caller is found.
- Temporarily retain the window file as the first stop and continue calling the issue a window-side boundary.

The second option was chosen at the time. The earlier investigation had already reached this file from the issue name and call name; if this location were also removed, later readers would have to start again from the vague term “release.” It was retained not because the window layer had been proven responsible, but because the existing traces of the investigation should not be lost.

That decision also implied a work sequence that later needed correction: first look for a sufficient explanation in the window file, then decide whether to trace the caller. This sequence mistook “a file that can be opened” for “a question that can be answered.” Subsequent review did not support that equivalence, so the old conclusion is retained here as it was, but is no longer a basis for closing the issue.

> Previous position: initially handle the buffer release boundary as a window-side issue; `MainWindow.xaml.cs` is the investigation starting point.
>
> Correction: it remains the investigation starting point, but is no longer considered the location for determining responsibility for the boundary.

## Fragments Actually Preserved in the File

What can currently be identified reliably is a few local positions in this file. Near the beginning, line 55 declares `namespace UndertaleModTool`. This places it in the application's window namespace, but the declaration itself does not provide the semantics of release.

There is resource access in the window code farther down:

```csharp
var resources = Application.Current.Resources;
```

This fragment is at line 265. Nearby, line 278 is:

```csharp
const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;
```

Farther down, line 332 opens a user registry class key:

```csharp
var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\Classes", true);
```

These fragments show that the old entry point did not arbitrarily point to a nonexistent file: this really is window code, and it contains local operations for resources, association changes, and registry handling. But they do not form a code path for “reading after buffer release.” Connecting them into such a path was an overinterpretation left by the initial draft.

Nearby binding names in the same file also include `UndertaleModTool`, `resources`, `long`, `HKCU_Classes`, `UndertaleModTool_app`, `ext`, and `args`. Some of these names are enough to help continue looking within the file for window initialization or association settings; they should not be used as substitutes for specific callers. In particular, `ext` and `args` are only binding names that can be located in this snapshot; the old record did not provide their relationship to the buffer object.

The role of the file location in this decision should therefore be narrowed to an “anchor for revisiting the investigation.” It preserves the direction taken by the earlier investigation and limits subsequent reading to a local area that can be checked, rather than packaging a series of nonadjacent pieces of window code as the release implementation.

## Later Addendum

In UMT-215, the verification item left later was specific: find a caller that still uses the “buffer release boundary,” and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. This verification item changed the focus of this record. The original question was “is the window file still worth examining”; it later became “which caller can provide the three facts needed to assess the boundary.”

The card also recorded that a design comparison had been performed, but the comparison was not developed here into a new conclusion about the mechanism. What can be confirmed is that the old window location was not directly promoted to resolved status at the time. A subsequent note also preserved the judgment made then:

> Don't close this yet; in the adaptive binary read boundary section, there is still one unconfirmed point for the buffer release boundary. Update it when the next fact comes in.

This sentence did not identify the specific call at the unconfirmed point, nor did it provide a runtime result. Its value lies in explicitly rejecting the reasoning that “the file has been found, so the issue is over.” The initial draft left only the entry point in the first half; the addendum documented the stopping point in the second half.

## Handling After Comparing the Options Again

During review, the possible approaches can be separated more clearly without inventing facts to fill in the old record.

The first approach is to continue treating the window file as the location responsible. The advantage is a short path, with no change to the old investigation name; the cost is that readers can easily infer a buffer chain from `Application.Current.Resources`, association-change constants, or registry access that does not actually exist in the record. This approach keeps the convenience of the initial draft, but amplifies the parts for which the draft had no evidence.

The second approach is to delete all window-side references, leaving only “waiting for a caller.” This would prevent the old wording from misleading readers, but would also discard the only existing file navigation. For people who still revisit the investigation through the historical issue name, this is worse than retaining an entry point with a correction.

The third approach is to retain the old label and file location while downgrading them from an attribution conclusion to search clues; the material actually used to assess the release boundary must come from a caller that still uses that boundary. The third approach was adopted after review.

This is not passing the issue off elsewhere. The window file should still be opened first, because the earlier investigation left visible traces here; but the reading objective has changed. Now the only requirement is to establish whether it can point to a specific call, rather than fully explain the buffer lifecycle here. If the file does not contain that connection, the next step is not to expand window-side speculation, but to follow the verification item and find the caller's version, entry point, and current result.

## Revised Decision

From now on, this record retains two levels and no longer mixes them.

1. “Window-side” is the old investigation label. It describes where the search historically began, not responsibility for the implementation.
2. `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is the file anchor that can currently be revisited. Lines 55, 265, 278, and 332 provide explicit reading locations, but do not provide the complete call relationships for release.
3. Whether there is a compatibility anomaly at the buffer release boundary depends on the caller that still uses that boundary and its actual version, entry point, and current result. If any one of these is missing, the status can only remain unconfirmed.

This revision also explains why the old file location is not replaced with another guessed module name. The input contains no second confirmed call entry point; substituting a path that looks more like a binary reading implementation would only create a new break in the historical trail. The old entry point can be retained, provided readers can see that it no longer serves an attribution role.

The state diagram below describes only the reading sequence permitted by this record, not the program's runtime states:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldIssueName
    OldIssueName --> MainWindowLocation
    MainWindowLocation --> CallerPendingVerification
    CallerPendingVerification --> RetainUMT_215
```

`MainWindowLocation` in the diagram is not a success state. It means the historical record can still take a review to the same file; the existing fragments cannot fill in the transition from here to “CallerPendingVerification.” `RetainUMT_215` likewise does not mean treating the card as an implementation description, but leaving the three facts from the actual environment that have not yet been obtained on the original verification item.

## The Old Entry Point That Still Applies

When revisiting the investigation through “buffer release boundary,” people can still open `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` first. First check whether clear call clues can be found near window-related bindings, resource access, association changes, or registry handling; if not, these adjacent fragments should not be treated as buffer evidence. This is where the value left by the old record ends.

If a candidate caller is found, its actual version, the entry point into that call, and the current result need to be recorded together. Only then can two completely different situations be distinguished: the window file was merely searched historically, or the window path really is still involved in triggering the issue. The initial draft did not have enough material to make this distinction, and the later addendum did not supply the answer for it either.

## The Remaining Item Not Split Off

“Adaptive binary read boundary” appears next to this issue in the addendum, but the two are not merged here. They may share the context of one investigation, or they may simply be two boundaries that remained unconfirmed in the same round; the existing record is insufficient to tell. The buffer release boundary continues to retain its own old label, file anchor, and caller verification item.

This page therefore remains a decision record from an earlier point in time, rather than new operating instructions. It corrects the scope of window-side attribution, but does not claim that the caller's version, entry point, or current result has been obtained.

title: Texture Pool and Tile Alignment Proposal

versions.body:
# Texture Pool and Tile Alignment Proposal

The interface review for the 2024.6 compatibility train starts by putting two issues in the same record: embedded texture pool counts and 2024.4 tile alignment. There is only one entry-point lead at present: `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. The file contains `namespace UndertaleModTool`, `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;`, `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;`, and registry read bindings, but these locations are not enough to establish where each issue's implementation belongs.

The initial proposal is to gather evidence in two passes, without combining the two results into a single pass criterion. The first route is to find an actual call for embedded texture pool counts and save the input used for that call and the result displayed by the tool. The second is to trigger 2024.4 tile alignment directly through the existing entry point and retain the input and actual output. This lets us distinguish “what the caller passed in” from “what the entry point produced” before deciding whether the interface needs adjustment.

There are two candidate approaches: trace back through the caller, which shows where the count and alignment parameters come from; or build a minimal reproduction through the entry point, which is easy to repeat but may bypass the real caller. Neither is being selected as the sole approach yet. If no actual call can be found, or the input fields cannot be confirmed, do not interpret an empty result as a compatibility failure. If the output differs from expectations, retain the original input and output first, then revert this round of interface changes.

versions.body:
# Texture Pool and Tile Alignment Plan

This proposal still covers both topics, but withdraws one premise from the previous version: embedded texture pool counting and 2024.4 tile alignment cannot be treated as the same interface issue merely because both investigations can start in the same place. The former needs the actual call behind a report, the input fields, and the result the user saw; the latter needs source code that can trigger the legacy alignment behavior, the input, and the tool's actual output. Each track is missing some material, and the gaps are different.

The existing source locations are still useful, but their purpose should be narrowed. `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is located in `namespace UndertaleModTool`, and the visible local points include `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;`, `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;`, and `var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\\Classes", true);`. These points show that this can serve as a starting point for tracing back: resource binding, file association, and window-side code are indeed visible in the same file. They do not explain how the embedded texture pool is counted, nor how the tiles in 2024.4 are arranged.

The path's role is therefore only to bring the investigation back to source code that can be inspected. It does not establish where the texture pool interface belongs, nor does it prove the tile conversion logic. If the actual call or triggering line found later is elsewhere, that new location should be used as the actual evidence; it need not lead back to this file to be valid. The presence of `resources`, `SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED`, or `HKCU_Classes` in the current file cannot be extrapolated to mean that texture objects, count fields, or tile data have already passed through those statements.

## No Shared Results Table This Time

The original idea was to put both issues into a single record: use the same column for input, the same column for returns, and the same column for pass status. This looks convenient for comparison, but would actually erase two kinds of differences. The input fields for texture counting have not yet been confirmed, so filling in a table first would only force the recorder to guess field names; tile alignment requires preserving the input and tool output before and after arrangement, rather than focusing on whether a returned object is non-null. Both tasks can be included in the same review, but their materials cannot substitute for each other.

The texture track must preserve at least three layers of facts separately. The first is the fields the caller actually passes to the interface; the second is the object or value returned by the interface; the third is the text or status the user sees in the tool. These three layers may or may not agree. Seeing a non-null object cannot directly be recorded as “there is one texture in the pool”; seeing displayed text also does not justify inferring that it must have come from the current entry point. Only by preserving the call location, input, and displayed result side by side can we determine which layer the “count” in the report actually refers to.

The tile track does not need to wait for the texture fields. It needs a minimal fixture that can be triggered directly through an existing entry point in the source code. The fixture's contents, dimensions, and specific fields are not currently provided in the record, so a sample must not be invented in advance just to speed things up. When it can be triggered, preserve the input's original order and the arrangement actually produced by the tool; when it cannot be triggered, record it as not triggered. If the tool output differs from expectations, preserve the output itself rather than rewriting it in the record as “already aligned” or “already fixed”.

Even when both tracks run at the same time, their results cannot be merged into one conclusion. Missing texture fields should not obscure output already obtained from the tile sample; differences in the tile sample's arrangement also cannot be attributed to the counting interface. The review should not ask “was this round an overall success”, but whether each track preserved enough input and results for reinspection. If one track stops, the other can continue collecting its own material.

## Embedded Texture Pool Counting: First Find the Call Corresponding to the Report

The local work left by UMT-217 is to find the actual call behind the latest report of “embedded texture pool counting” and fill in how it was called and what the user saw. This requirement is stricter than “finding a similar name”. The issue name, call name, and implementation ownership may all differ; a snippet with a similar name alone cannot establish whether it produced the count in the report, nor confirm which fields the caller supplied.

Candidate path A is caller-first. First pin down the call location corresponding to the latest report, and transcribe only the fields the caller actually passed and the displayed result after the call completed. The count value, whether a returned object exists, and the text shown in the UI should be in separate columns; they must not be merged into a single Boolean judgment in the first round of records. Path A's value is that it can answer who consumes the interface; the cost is that, if the fields' origins remain unclear, tracing back will stop at the call boundary.

Path A does not require immediate changes to the interface. After finding the call, first confirm that the record concerns that same call, not another branch that also retrieves a texture object. The call location must be paired with the saved input; retaining only a line number or only a screenshot-like result cannot substantiate the counting semantics. If the call's input is incomplete, missing items should be explicitly left blank, not replaced with local resource-binding or registry-reading code.

Candidate path B is entry-point-first. Choose a minimal input that can be processed directly through the existing tool entry point, preserve the original input, interface return, and UI result separately, then compare them with path A's call sample. This is suitable for obtaining a reproducible local sample while the fields are not yet fully confirmed, and can also help identify cases where “the entry point is stable, but the reported call is different”. It cannot prove that the call in the report necessarily used the same fields, much less independently establish the externally visible meaning of the pool count.

Path B's limits must be stated clearly. A minimal input producing a result through the entry point does not mean it covers the caller involved in the actual report; no anomaly in the UI also does not mean the count comes from the same object. If path B returns a different object from path A, preserve that difference first and pause any attempt to merge the two into a single interface conclusion. What needs to be filled in at that point is the call relationship or field origins, not a declaration that one sample is the baseline.

Paths A and B both produce comparable material, but they answer different questions. A answers how the consumer in the report retrieves values; B answers what the existing entry point produces for a minimal input. The proposal does not require them to match immediately; even if they match, confirmation of the input fields cannot be skipped. Only when the call locations, inputs, and results displayed by the tool can be compared item by item should we discuss whether these two observations need to be grouped into the same compatibility judgment.

## The Field Blocker Changed the Sequence

UMT-217 moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-10-16, then to Blocked the next day; the recorded reason was that the upstream interface owner had not yet confirmed the input fields. This status change is not a progress note, but a stopping point for the texture track. While the fields remain unconfirmed, continuing to define counting semantics would only put assumptions ahead of the material. The previous arrangement of “write a call sample first and fill in the fields later” is no longer being used.

This does not mean there is nothing left to do on the texture work. We can continue locating the actual call referenced by the report, prepare the record structure, and distinguish the returned object from the result displayed to the user; but unknown fields cannot be assumed to be zero, null, or a default configuration. Any count obtained using those defaults is excluded from the final compatibility assessment and cannot serve as a reason for adjusting the interface.

Once the upstream fields are confirmed, the sequence for resuming path A should remain restrained: first verify that the call really corresponds to the report, then preserve the fields actually passed, and finally record the result the user saw. The call's identity must not be left unverified just because the fields have finally become available. Field confirmation only resolves “what is the input”, not automatically “does this input belong to the call in the latest report”.

If field confirmation remains delayed, path B can continue as a local entry-point experiment, but its conclusions must be limited to entry-point behavior. It can show what a defined input produces after passing through the existing tool, but cannot fill in the actual calling method for UMT-217. Elevating B's result into a conclusion about the counting interface is a shortcut this proposal explicitly rejects.

## 2024.4 Tile Alignment: Keep the Input and Arrangement Together

The requirement from UMT-219 is more direct: run source code that can trigger “2024.4 tile alignment” through the existing entry point, and save the input and the tool's actual output. The difficulty here is not whether the tool can open the file, but whether the original arrangement is preserved after legacy data enters the entry point. An ordinary resource-binding snippet cannot automatically serve as a tile sample; only source code that actually triggers the alignment behavior satisfies this track's starting requirement.

The minimal fixture's goal should be narrow: make the alignment behavior occur, rather than construct a large sample covering every resource scenario. Once the input is determined, its original order must be preserved in the record. The tool output must likewise be saved in its actual order so that any arrangement changes can be seen later. The expected arrangement has not yet been frozen, so this proposal cannot present any particular arrangement as the established correct answer.

If the first input does not trigger alignment, it should not be disguised as “alignment unchanged”. Not being triggered means the sample is not yet an entry point for that behavior; the record should retain that status, and the search should continue for source code that reaches the behavior directly. If it has been triggered but the output is unexpected, do not fold that output into a texture-counting failure either. It is an observation belonging to the tile track and should be preserved together with the original input.

The tile track can finish a round of material collection before the texture track because it does not depend on the input fields missing from UMT-217. This ordering does not mean the tile issue is more important, nor that its results can replace texture validation; the two tasks simply have different blocking conditions at present. If tile results appear first, the review can first discuss whether the arrangement differences require further investigation, without waiting for the texture field issue to be resolved.

Putting the texture sample and tile fixture into the same run can only save preparation time; it cannot create a joint pass condition. A joint condition would lead to two misreadings: blank fields on the texture track might be incorrectly recorded as a tile issue, and differences in tile output might be incorrectly recorded as instability in the counting interface. The record format should allow readers to extract either track's input, output, and unresolved items independently.

## Changes Not Being Submitted Yet

The current material is insufficient to directly change the interface semantics of embedded texture pool counting. Without the actual call and confirmed fields, any statement about “what the count should be” would go beyond the available evidence. It is also currently insufficient to specify new arrangement rules for 2024.4 tile alignment; UMT-219 asks for the input and the tool's actual output to be saved, not for a fixed result to be assumed in advance.

This means the first deliverables from this round of work are two local records that can be reinspected, not a joint change. The texture record must contain at least the call location, actual input fields, returned object or value, and the result the user saw. The tile record must contain at least the source code that can trigger the behavior, the original input order, and the tool's actual output. Blank items in both records must remain as they are; filling gaps with material from the other track would create false associations.

`MainWindow.xaml.cs` can still be listed as a search entry point, but not as proof of the implementation in the deliverables. The existing resource, constant, and registry locations in the file only help return to the area that was inspectable at the time. They cannot be used to determine the number of members in the texture pool, nor the alignment result for legacy tiles. If a more direct call or triggering line is found later, that direct location should replace this broader entry-point clue.

## This Round's Choice and Withdrawal Conditions

The choice is to prepare in parallel and interpret separately. Texture counting first waits for field confirmation while continuing to search for the actual call corresponding to the report; tile alignment first searches for a minimal fixture that can trigger the behavior and saves the input and actual output. Neither track is designated as a prerequisite for the other.

In the following situations, withdraw the corresponding judgment rather than fill gaps with speculation:

- If only the issue name or a similar call name is found, but not the actual call corresponding to the report, withdraw the interface judgment for texture counting.
- While input fields remain unconfirmed, do not submit counting-semantics changes or interpret blank fields as zero.
- If the entry-point sample returns a result but cannot be linked to the actual call, retain only the entry-point observation; do not record it as the caller's result.
- If the tile input cannot be triggered through the source-code entry point, retain the not-triggered record; do not substitute a texture sample.
- If tile behavior has been triggered but the input and tool output were not saved together, do not use that run's result to judge arrangement compatibility.
- Discuss whether there is a shared follow-up interface adjustment only when each track's material can be reviewed independently.

Only two previous judgments are retained. First, `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs` is a valuable starting point for tracing back; second, both issues can be tracked in the same compatibility train review. The judgment being withdrawn is that “the same entry point is enough for them to share evidence and conclusions”. Having the same entry point only means the search starts in nearby places, not that the inputs, objects, or failure manifestations are the same.

The items that remain undetermined should also stay at the end of the proposal rather than be prematurely resolved. The actual call, input fields, returned object, and specific result the user saw for embedded texture pool counting still need to be filled in. The source code that can trigger 2024.4 tile alignment, the minimal fixture's contents, and the expected arrangement are also not defined by the existing material. Until field confirmation resumes for UMT-217, the texture track will advance only source location work and record preparation; UMT-219 will continue collecting an independent sample, limited to the input and the tool's actual output.

# DDS Image Interpolation Troubleshooting Tree

When the image state is abnormal, first record DDS mipmap consumption and explicit image interpolation separately. Both can occur around the same operation, but do not treat them as a single cause without enough observed evidence.

```
Abnormal image result
├─ Appears only after processing DDS
│  └─ Record whether mipmap consumption occurred, along with any return value or raw diagnostics captured at the time
└─ Appears after interpolation is explicitly specified
   └─ Record whether the interpolation setting was actually triggered through the user-facing path
```

Do not confirm the behavior only through the debug entry point. Retrace the steps to the failure through normal UI operations; if it does not reproduce through that path, retain that finding and do not treat the debug-entry result as a confirmed compatibility issue.

Start the source-code trace at `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. This is a window-side location to start from: `namespace UndertaleModTool` is at line 55, and `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;` is at line 265. Resource access alone does not establish that DDS data has been read or that interpolation has taken effect; continue tracing the references actually triggered to confirm.

If there is only a visual difference, with no return value or raw diagnostics, stop at recording the observed behavior. Do not modify the DDS path on that basis, and do not mark the interpolation check as passed.

# DDS Image Interpolation Troubleshooting Tree

When image results are abnormal, first split the situation into two tracks: the state after DDS mipmap consumption, and the actual trigger after the caller explicitly specifies image interpolation. They may occur during the same window operation, but adjacent names do not mean the processing happens in the same place. A visual change that appears first also cannot replace confirmation of the consumption action or interpolation setting.

Start troubleshooting from the user's routine calls. First record whether this operation interacts with DDS or another image object; then record the stage at which the abnormality becomes visible, before or after mipmap consumption; finally record whether there was an action that explicitly specified interpolation. Keep any available return values or raw diagnostics as well. If diagnostics are unavailable, state directly that there are no raw diagnostics, rather than filling in a cause based on visual impressions.

```text
Start: Abnormal image results in the user path
|
+-- Can it be confirmed that the current object involves a DDS payload?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Was image interpolation explicitly specified?
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- Yes: Record the setting action and the user path actually taken.
|   |   |   `-- No: Keep the image object and observed behavior on record; do not include them in this workflow.
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Did mipmap consumption occur in this path?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes: Keep the post-consumption state and any available return values or raw diagnostics.
|       |   `-- Unclear: Repeat the same user path; do not use a debug entry point to fill in a conclusion.
|       |
|       `-- Was interpolation also explicitly specified?
|           |
|           +-- Yes: Record DDS and interpolation separately; do not combine them into a single cause.
|           `-- No: Stop after completing the trace-back for the DDS branch.
|
`-- Insufficient input or diagnostics
    `-- Stop making changes and release decisions, and log the missing items.
```

## Recording the Situation

For the same reproduction, distinguish at least three facts: “the object has entered DDS processing,” “mipmap consumption is confirmed,” and “abnormal image results are visible.” The first fact does not imply the other two; the third fact also cannot establish which specific step occurred. If all that is known is that the post-processing state is abnormal, it can serve as the starting point for the DDS branch, but it cannot be used to choose a recovery action.

Record explicit interpolation in the same way. Keep a record of the action that sets interpolation and the path actually reached after that action. Seeing the check execute only in an example or debug entry point shows only that this entry point can trigger the check; it must not be recorded as coverage of normal UI operations. If the user path does not pass through this check, keep the uncovered path on record, rather than letting a local observation from DDS close it out.

When the abnormality involves both tracks, record events in the order they occurred, rather than replacing all observations with “the image changed.” First record whether the DDS object has entered mipmap consumption, then whether interpolation was explicitly specified, and finally when the abnormality became visible. If the order cannot be confirmed, keep only the shared observed behavior and the missing observation points; do not first change one part of the processing in the hope of getting lucky.

Failure to reproduce on the routine path is also worth recording. It means the current review has not reproduced the debug entry point's behavior through normal operations, not that the problem has disappeared. Conversely, an abnormality that is consistently visible in the debug entry point can only be used to continue locating references and objects; it cannot directly establish a compatibility assessment.

## DDS Branch

After confirming that the object involves DDS, first ask whether mipmap consumption actually occurred during this user operation. If it can be confirmed, keep the post-consumption state, return values, or raw diagnostics; if only a difference in the final image is visible and there is no return information that can be retained, stop at describing the state. Do not infer from visual differences that the consumption logic has completed, and do not record this result as an interpolation check failure.

Repeating the DDS branch should use the same user entry point. Sending the object separately into a debug entry point may help confirm that the object can be processed, but it cannot prove that normal operations in the window take the same path. If the issue reproduces through the routine entry point, prioritize recording the facts that occurred there; if it does not reproduce through the routine entry point, record its results and the debug entry point's results separately, rather than blending them into one conclusion.

If diagnostics cannot be obtained either before or after mipmap consumption, do not expand the troubleshooting scope further. Simply record the object type, the known stage, and the missing output. Do not switch to modifying explicit interpolation just because it is “image-related,” and do not use results from an interpolation example to explain the DDS state.

## Explicit Image Interpolation Branch

The interpolation branch must answer whether the caller explicitly requested interpolation and whether that request reached the existing check through a user operation. The presence of some image processing in the code does not answer either question. First locate the setting action, then follow this window operation to confirm the subsequent path; if the setting appears only in an example, record it as an example result, without extending it to coverage of the user path.

Sometimes a DDS object and an interpolation setting appear together. In that case, both records can proceed in parallel, but each must retain its own trigger conditions and diagnostics. An abnormality after DDS processing does not automatically prove that the interpolation setting was read; execution of the interpolation check also does not automatically prove that the mipmap has been consumed. If either track lacks input, the other track's results cannot fill that gap.

If the interpolation setting is explicit but the user path has no subsequent state that can be retained, stop at “setting triggered, result unconfirmed.” This is more accurate than directly marking the existing check as passed. Uncovered user paths remain in UMT-222; this window-side trace-back does not replace them.

## Starting the Trace-Back from the Window Side

The window-side entry point is `UndertaleModTool/MainWindow.xaml.cs`. Known locations include `namespace UndertaleModTool` on line 55, `var resources = Application.Current.Resources;` on line 265, and `const long SHCNE_ASSOCCHANGED = 0x08000000;` on line 278. These locations are useful for mapping the abnormality back to references near normal UI operations, but resource access and association-change constants themselves are not evidence of DDS consumption or interpolation taking effect.

Continuing downward, `var HKCU_Classes = Registry.CurrentUser.OpenSubKey(@"Software\Classes", true);` on line 332 and the adjacent application association handling may also appear in the same window context after startup. They only help confirm the window environment in which the operation takes place. Until the image object has been located by following references, do not classify registry access, resource dictionaries, or file association changes as causes of the image abnormality.

Keep the trace-back sequence close to this operation: first confirm which image object the window action obtained; then confirm whether that object carries DDS data; next check whether it enters mipmap consumption; finally confirm whether there is an explicit interpolation setting. If the references cease to connect to the operation being investigated along the way, stop there and attach the recorded behavior next to the point where the connection breaks. Do not guess where the object goes in other modules just to obtain a complete chain.

The window side is not responsible for all image assessments either. It provides locations near the UI entry point; starting here does not justify attributing DDS processing to the window file. What is needed is a reference connecting the current operation to the object, not a declaration that looks related to an image problem.

## Cards and Blocked Status

UMT-221 focuses on abnormal states after DDS mipmap consumption. When handling it, ensure this consumption occurs through the user's routine calls, and keep the return values or raw diagnostics. If only visual behavior is obtained locally, with no diagnostics that can be retained, record that gap as well; do not make a release decision based solely on the local display.

UMT-222 uses existing tests or examples to trigger explicit image interpolation and records uncovered user paths back on the card. Tests or examples can confirm trigger conditions, but they do not replace reproduction through normal window operations. After an example proves that the call exists, it is still necessary to check whether the user will pass through the same check.

During subsequent review, work related to DDS was handled under the release classification; the CI queue then became blocked, and the local results were not used further for subsequent assessments. A blocked queue is neither evidence that the DDS state has recovered nor evidence that the interpolation check failed. If the same situation occurs, record only what the local results can establish and the fact that the CI queue is blocked, and stop advancing release conclusions when CI results are missing.

Do not combine the blocked CI with debug entry point results to conclude that it passed. The former lacks subsequent verification, while the latter lacks confirmation through routine calls; retain these two gaps separately. When resuming the review, first fill in the records connected to this user path, then decide which branch can continue.

## Stop Conditions

A troubleshooting run can end at any branch point. The closing record only needs to state clearly: whether the issue reproduced on the user path, whether DDS and mipmap consumption can be confirmed, whether explicit interpolation can be confirmed, what return values or raw diagnostics were retained, and whether the blocker is missing input, a broken reference chain, or the CI queue.

If the abnormality appears only in the debug entry point, list that separately rather than folding it into the routine path's results. DDS and interpolation can continue separately in different rounds; a common cause does not have to be established in the same round. Missing texture dimensions are a related issue, see DOC-23; results there cannot replace confirmation here of the consumption state or interpolation trigger.

The old notes treated this neighboring code as part of the search context. Looking back, it explains why the main window file seemed so busy, but it provides no point where texture dimensions are used. Continuing to search through association registration, extensions, or argument branches risks misrepresenting startup handling as resource handling.

The old entry point is preserved as it was: first go to the main window file, confirm where resources are obtained, then check whether the old notes put the application resource object and the dimension issue together. Stop there. This entry point no longer serves to infer the source of dimensions from the window.

```text
Old records
Issue name / call name
      |
      v
Near the resources in MainWindow.xaml.cs
      |
      +-- Retained as a historical entry point

After migration
Caller still using dimension information
      |
      v
Actual version + entry point + result of this check
      |
      v
Main window entry point used only for historical comparison
```

The starting point after migration comes from UMT-223: first find a caller that still uses “missing texture dimensions,” then verify its actual version, how that usage point is reached, and the result of this check. The results do not need to be reduced to a single uniform status. Dimensions still missing, dimensions already present, and unable to determine at that entry point are distinct results that should be recorded as they are.

In practice, first confirm that the location found actually uses dimension information. Then record the version being checked; do not use the filename of `MainWindow.xaml.cs` as evidence of the version. This migration does not exclude the window side from the investigation. The old notes placed the resource object and the dimension issue together, which is necessary context for later readers to understand the judgment made at the time. Removing it would instead suggest that the old investigation had more direct evidence. The only change is which record takes priority: the window side retains the old search entry point, while the caller side records the usage point actually examined in this round of compatibility checks.

The resource-initialization hypothesis from the first draft is retained here, but it should no longer be a reason to expand the search scope.

When the new entry point cannot yet produce a result, the old path can be used again for historical comparison—for example, if the caller is absent from the version being checked, or the entry point cannot be reproduced. Returning to the old path does not mean undoing the new record: retain the reason the caller-side check stopped, then return to the resource acquisition location to check the old notes. Sprite mask row storage is not part of this migration; DOC-24 retain the other subject checked in that round. The two issue names in the same compatibility effort cannot share a call chain on that basis.

# Spine Texture State Decision Record

In the 2024.6 compatibility train, retain the Spine texture state as a compatibility issue rather than reducing it to a conclusion that the sprite model did or did not handle it. The existing investigation entry is `UndertaleModLib/Models/UndertaleSprite.cs`; it is useful for revisiting model adjacency and prior conclusions, but it is not enough on its own to show whether the state difference arose during reading, saving, or display.

The initial draft compared two approaches. The first was to classify the state difference in the report directly as an ordinary texture compatibility issue. Its advantage was the small scope of change; its drawback was losing the Spine qualifier. The second was to retain the state name, add records around a reproducible sample, and then decide whether the model needed to change. The second approach was adopted.

The reason for this choice is not that the model file is unimportant, but that there was no material at the time that could connect the sample result to a specific object in the model. If the issue is first assumed to be in a field, construction step, or conversion branch, later reading can easily focus only on material that supports that judgment. Saving the sample first lets subsequent decisions return to the same phenomenon and avoids conflating the existence of a resource with the correctness of the result.

The objects that need to be retained are a sample that shows the difference, the failure text or output bytes from that time, and the sample’s verification relationship with `UndertaleSprite.cs`. Both the failure text and the output bytes can serve as material for later comparison; the former is suited to preserving one readable failure, while the latter is suited to pinning down results that text alone cannot distinguish. They are not two fixed artifacts that must be collected together.

This decision does not require expanding immediately to all sprite paths. The fact that the resource can find the texture does not mean that the reported state difference has disappeared; conversely, different output bytes alone cannot identify the difference as having occurred during saving. The sample bounds the issue first, and code reading then determines which relationships are worth tracing further.

It has not yet been decided which object should own the state, nor whether a new conversion branch is needed. The next review will first verify the sample’s result in the current version, then return to the model path to check the relevant declarations and adjacent processing. If a later sample only demonstrates an ordinary texture difference, separate it from the Spine qualifier discussed in this record.
